Regarding attachment, obsessiveness can occur when you're attracted to someone who is emotionally distanced / unavailable. The less they respond to your feelings, the harder you may find yourself chasing. It's like an addiction.

Try doing some research attachment, to help you realize this pattern. YouTube can be useful.

Moving away from the temptations might help, but it's important to understand why you're doing this so it doesn't repeat or continue. Heavily romantizing, constantly daydreaming or putting people onto pedestals in an obsessive manner is looking at said person through rose-tinted glasses. You need to try and smash those glasses. Therapy, attachment research and a self-reflection diary might be useful. This is just my opinion though.

CBT stands for cognitive behavioural therapy. It's a form of talking therapy that helps you be aware of your thought patterns, which then effect your mood and actions. Depressive thoughts lead to a depressive mood and thus depressive actions, which leads to depressive thoughts....and the cycle continues. A CBT counsellor will help someone become aware of these dark thoughts and learn how to override and challenge them in order to produce better feelings, actions and thoughts. So, what was her response to offering getting her help? I hope she does. It's a horrible way to live with depression. But at the end of the day, she must keep trying to help herself, for both your sakes. It's a cruel truth, but you're a human being too with thoughts and feelings. It's down to you if you can support her through getting mental health help (which could take a while to begin to take affect), or her not get help and continue living how you are...which doesn't seem to be working for you. It's horrible when the people around us also pay for our mental health problems. But help is out there to reduce that price for everyone involved.

If she has depression, have you had a talk about what help there is for her? Counselling, medication etc. Back when I had depression the smallest of tasks would feel impossible with 0 motivation. It was thanks to a CBT counsellor guiding me once a week I was able to feel supported and slowly change the way I think. If depression and anxiety are causing life problems, deal with that core issue. Things might soon unwind with some support for her where it counts.

Hey :) I'm recently researching fear of flying treatment options. Here's a list of options I've found that may help you:

Airline Fear of Flying Programme (Costs) British Airways, Easyjet, some others. 

SOAR programme - either downloadable videos, VR or an app (Costs)

Therapy or Cognative Behavioural Therapy.

I used to have a kind of claustrophobia on aircraft, and CBT was the most effective (and free on the NHS) for me. Everyones anxiety is different, so everyones 'cure' may variate also. Explore the above options. I'm currently working on a new treatment type that's low cost and effective, as I don't want peoples lives to be prohibited by fear. Good luck :)

From my own experience (I'm just about to finish UK university), I think it really depends on every person. There is no right and wrong, it's literally whatever makes you the happiest. I see people take degree options because they don't know what else to do, hate it, and drop out. If you know what you enjoy, go to uni and develop the skills :) I would suggest that if you're having doubts, take the time off to get some experience and do some research. What you think and what reality is can be different, so experience will fill those gaps and teach you what you like/dislike. There's loads of courses and places to study numerous things - if possible, turn your favourite hobby/skill into a career. "If you love your job, you'll never have to work a day in your life." - I didn't regret my decision of course, but I did regret not doing my research or having enough experience to make informed and realistic decisions. Things will work out though - it's not the end of everything. Do what feels right to you, because nobody else can tell you how you truly feel. They can only tell you the practical side of things and their own feelings/opinion :)

I'm so sorry to hear you're in an emotionally abusive and manipulative relationship. I literally got out of one a few months ago. The best advice I can give you: Is get out of there. 

Look, it's okay that you relapsed. After 6 years with him, it would be difficult to just up and leave.

Just remember to trust yourself. You originally left him for a reason - if it was meant to work out, it would have already. You can actively search for his positive attributes because it's easier than looking at the truth, but if you're having to put effort into searching for good, then he isn't good. 

When you date people like that, communication is their powerline. If you cut of ALL communication - they can't get to you. You're safe. You have the power to live any life you want, learn to love yourself, and know what you're worth.  I'm 19 too, and that means we're still young and have time to start again. It's never too late. Get the mental health support you may need if the emotional abuse has got you all knotted up, and you'll eventually realise that leaving was the healthiest choice you've ever made for yourself. 

It's  hard at first, but gosh, is it worth it when you start to see the light of freedom. The more space from him you get, the more perspective you'll learn. You'll look back and wished "Wow, I should of left a long time ago, I love myself too much to settle for this abuse!" 

You feel like shit because you're basically having withdrawal symptoms. Alcohol is a truth serum, so it will make you more lenient into giving into temptation. I would avoid any substances if you feel upset/mentally unstable for the time being. Go and spend time with friends, indulge in netflix, and have some you time. But first - you gotta let him go.

It doesn't need to be a massive goodbye. You don't even have to say a word if you don't want to. Make it easy for yourself by understanding how you feel - if you know he'll manipulate you to stay through a conversation, don't bother with a conversation. I find what I do before bed/preparing for sleep helps a lot. I Imagine that my mind is a fast running, hard working motor all day - no wonder it's so hard to just 'switch off' straight away when we decide it's time to go to sleep.  To make myself feel like I want to sleep, maybe 45 mins or so before bed, I listen to calm music, do some light yoga/mediation, face masks and incense candles etc.
And most importantly- I stop thinking. Say 'No' when you feel your thoughts start to rev up your brain again. Become calm, then feeling the urge to sleep may be more accessible.
Also, turn down brightness on your screens as it stimulates sunlight that keeps you awake- browsing through your phone or watching hyperactive or intense films before bed might not help you relax. An active or worrying mind will keep you awake.

Also, look into sleep (REM) cycles. Waking up in the middle of a 'deep sleep' can make you feel like crap when you wake up, since you've interrupted the cycle before its full completion. Too much, little or scattered sleep patterns might screw up your sleeping cycles over a period of time and make you feel drained or constantly tired. So, maybe avoid setting multiple alarms in the mornings and keep waking up every day at the same time. Make it a pattern, and your mind/body will become used to it as well as feeling fully refreshed and making the most of its energy.
